items.prompt: A type scale multiplies a base size by a fixed ratio at each step, e.g. 16px ×1.25 → 20px ×1.25 → 25px. What does using a fixed ratio buy you that picking sizes one at a time doesn't, per L2?
choices: Faster overall page load times for the visitor, since a fixed multiplier is computationally cheaper to render than ad hoc sizes
Consistency you don't have to re-justify — a new heading level slots in at the next multiple without a fresh judgment call
It fully and automatically guarantees the resulting text will pass a WCAG contrast check with no further verification needed
It entirely removes the underlying need for any deliberate spacing at all between the various elements on the page
items.explanation: L2's guiding question on type scale is answered directly: a fixed multiplier means a 5th heading level or a second unrelated page built from the same scale stays consistent without a new by-eye decision each time.
items.reference:
16px body
×1.25 → 20px
×1.25 → 25px

Why: a fixed ratio applied repeatedly, not sizes picked one at a time — consistency you don't have to re-justify.
items.learnMore:
Ratios compound

A type scale multiplies a base size by a fixed ratio at each step. base × ratio^steps. At ratio 1.25 over 3 steps: 16 × 1.25³ ≈ 31px. At ratio 1.05 over 3 steps: 16 × 1.05³ ≈ 18.5px — barely distinct from body text.

Common mistake

Picking heading sizes by eye, one at a time. It looks fine per-heading and inconsistent the moment two live on the same page.

items.prompt: Per L2's WCAG formula, luminance is computed as L = 0.2126·R + 0.7152·G + 0.0722·B (on linearized channels). Why does this explain a saturated blue button looking 'loud' but still failing a contrast check?
choices: Blue, in this particular formula, always happens to carry the single highest weight of the three, so it should pass easily
The formula weights green far more heavily (0.7152) than blue (0.0722), so a color that looks visually loud due to saturation can still have low measured luminance if it's blue-dominant
The underlying WCAG luminance formula, as written, genuinely doesn't include any term at all for the blue color channel
Perceived visual loudness and measured luminance are, in this particular framing, actually the exact same measurement
items.explanation: L2 calls out this exact gap: perceived brightness and measured luminance are different axes, and the formula's heavy green weighting versus blue's tiny 0.0722 weighting is precisely why a vivid blue can look attention-grabbing yet contribute little measured luminance.
items.reference:
Normal text4.5:1 (AA) / 7:1 (AAA)
Large text3:1 (AA) / 4.5:1 (AAA)
UI components3:1

Why: contrast ratio = (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05) on WCAG relative luminance — a real number, checked against a real threshold.
items.learnMore:
The formula, in three steps
StepComputes
1Linearize each RGB channel (gamma correction)
2L = 0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B
3ratio = (lighter L + 0.05) / (darker L + 0.05)

#767676 on white computes to ≈4.54:1 — passes AA normal text by a hair, fails AAA.

Common mistake

Judging contrast by eye. Perceived brightness and measured luminance aren't the same axis — green is weighted far higher (0.7152) than blue (0.0722).

items.learnMore:
Proximity is a grouping signal

Humans perceptually group nearby elements before consciously reading their content — this is why unrelated fields with equal spacing read as one undifferentiated list, and why the fix is purely a spacing change, not new dividers or labels.

items.prompt: L3 works the WCAG formula for #767676 text on a white background and arrives at ≈4.54:1. What does L3 say about this result?
choices: It comfortably and easily passes both the AA threshold and the AAA threshold here, with plenty of margin left to spare
It clears the AA minimum (4.5:1) by a tiny margin and fails AAA (7:1) outright — a color that 'looked fine' turns out to pass by the thinnest margin
It fails the AA threshold entirely here and needs to be replaced immediately before this particular design can ship at all
This particular calculation is, in this framing, said to be only a rough approximation that can't be trusted for real decisions
items.explanation: L3's worked example lands at 4.54:1, just 0.04 over the 4.5:1 AA floor — the unit's point is that this margin is uncomfortably thin (rounding-error thin) even though the color visually 'looked fine,' and it fails AAA outright.
items.reference:
Normal text4.5:1 (AA) / 7:1 (AAA)
Large text3:1 (AA) / 4.5:1 (AAA)
UI components3:1

Why: contrast ratio = (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05) on WCAG relative luminance — a real number, checked against a real threshold.
items.learnMore:
The formula, in three steps
StepComputes
1Linearize each RGB channel (gamma correction)
2L = 0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B
3ratio = (lighter L + 0.05) / (darker L + 0.05)

#767676 on white computes to ≈4.54:1 — passes AA normal text by a hair, fails AAA.

Common mistake

Judging contrast by eye. Perceived brightness and measured luminance aren't the same axis — green is weighted far higher (0.7152) than blue (0.0722).

Because the three weights sum to 1, and when R, G, and B are equal, the weighted sum collapses to that same single linearized value regardless of how it's split among the weights
Because gray colors specifically are, in this particular framing, said to be entirely excluded from the WCAG formula altogether
Because gray, as a color, is said in this particular framing to always carry a fixed luminance of exactly 0.5 by definition
items.explanation: L3 notes this explicitly: since 0.2126 + 0.7152 + 0.0722 = 1 and R = G = B for gray, the weighted sum reduces to that single equal value — no need to separately weight three identical numbers.

items.prompt: L3's redesign runs three passes in order: spacing, then type scale, then color/contrast. What reason does L3 give for checking contrast last?
choices: Contrast is, in this particular framing, considered the single least important of the four levers, so it's saved for last
Grouping/hierarchy problems are usually cheaper to fix than contrast problems, so finding and fixing them first avoids re-verifying a color choice against a layout that's about to be restructured
Colors, as a rule, must always be deliberately picked only after every single piece of text has already been fully finalized
There's genuinely no real underlying reason for this at all — the order here is arbitrary and could be reversed at no cost
items.explanation: L3 explains the ordering as a cost-avoidance choice: structural passes (spacing, hierarchy) are likely to change the layout, so verifying contrast — which is a checking step, not a structural one — makes more sense once the structure has settled.
items.reference:
① Spacing — group for free
② Type scale — signal priority
③ Contrast — verify with math

Why: grouping/hierarchy problems are usually cheaper to fix than contrast problems, so finding them first avoids re-verifying color on a layout about to be restructured.
items.learnMore:
Why this order, not another

Spacing and type-scale passes are structural — they change what the layout communicates. A contrast pass is a verification step on colors that may still move if the layout changes. Doing verification last avoids re-checking a color choice against a spacing/hierarchy structure that hasn't stabilized yet.

Common mistake

Polishing exact colors before the layout structure (grouping, hierarchy) is settled, then having to redo the color pass after a later structural change.

items.prompt: L3 gives an example of a bright mint-green brand color (#7FE8C4) computing to roughly 1.4:1 contrast as text on white. What workable pattern does L3 suggest instead of abandoning the brand color?
choices: Simply never use that particular brand color anywhere at all throughout the entire rest of the product going forward

Keep the literal brand value as a fill/accent (badge background, icon, border) where the contrast bar is lower or absent, and use a darker or lighter tint of the same hue anywhere it needs to carry text
Simply increase the font size being used until the contrast ratio requirement itself no longer technically applies at all
Contrast rules, as a general rule, are said in this framing to genuinely not apply at all to a product's own brand colors
items.explanation: L3's recommended pattern separates use cases: the literal brand hue works fine where contrast thresholds are looser (fills, accents, badges) but needs a tint adjustment anywhere it has to function as legible text.
items.reference:
Brand hue as text
Brand hue as fill/accent

Why: a light saturated brand color often fails contrast as text but works fine as a badge fill or icon, where the threshold is looser or doesn't apply.
items.learnMore:
Brand color vs. contrast floor

A light, saturated brand hue (e.g. a bright mint) can have a luminance close to white's, producing a contrast ratio near 1:1 as text on a light background — nowhere near the 3:1 floor for UI components, let alone 4.5:1 for text. The workable pattern: keep the literal brand value as a fill/accent where the bar is lower or absent, and use a darker or lighter tint of the same hue anywhere it needs to carry text.

Common mistake

Treating "it's the brand color" as an exemption from the contrast floor instead of a constraint to design around with tints.

items.prompt: Per L3's edge cases, how should a dense data table with 40 rows on screen handle the spacing lever, given that a full 8px rhythm may cost more vertical space than it can afford?
choices: Skip the spacing rhythm lever entirely for any dense table like this one, since it's said in this framing to simply not apply here
Still apply a step scale, just a finer one (e.g. 4px instead of 8px), so rows stay legibly separated without spending the vertical budget a form doesn't have to worry about
Use the exact same unmodified 8px spacing scale here as would be used on any ordinary form, with absolutely no adjustment made
Remove all spacing between the individual rows entirely here, purely in order to fit as many total rows onto the screen as possible
items.explanation: L3 is explicit that the spacing lever still applies to dense tables — it doesn't get skipped — but the step size shrinks (e.g. to 4px) to respect the tighter vertical budget a data-dense view has to work within.
items.reference:
📊 Dense tables — smaller spacing step, not zero
🎨 Color alone ≠ a valid signal
🖼️ Contrast must match the real rendered background

Why: every lever still applies at the edges — the scale or context just has to adapt to the real constraint.
items.learnMore:
Levers still apply, values shift

A dense data table doesn't get to skip spacing rhythm — it uses a finer step (e.g. 4px instead of 8px) so rows stay separated without costing the vertical space a table can't spare. Color-coded states (red = error, green = success) need a second non-color cue (icon or text) for readers who can't distinguish hue, per WCAG 1.4.1 — that's independent of whether the colors themselves pass contrast. And a contrast check is only valid against the actual rendered background — a translucent card over a variable photo can pass against its own nominal fill and still fail once the real image renders under it.

Common mistake

Checking contrast against a solid nominal background color when the real background is an image or gradient that varies in lightness across its area.

items.prompt: L3 asks what would need to be redone for a dark theme where the background flips from white to near-black. Per the WCAG formula, what actually changes?
choices: Nothing at all changes here — a gray value that already passes comfortably against a white background automatically passes against black too
The ratio must be recomputed with the new background's luminance, and which color is 'lighter' (L1) vs. 'darker' (L2) in the formula may flip — the old pass doesn't carry over automatically
Only the specific font being used needs to change here; the underlying contrast math itself is said to stay completely identical
Dark themes, as a category, are said in this particular framing to be entirely exempt from WCAG's contrast requirements altogether
items.explanation: L3's extension question makes clear that flipping the background swaps the roles in the ratio formula and requires fresh computation — a gray that comfortably passed against white isn't guaranteed to pass, or fail, the same way against a dark background.
items.reference:
🌙 Dark theme — recompute, don't assume the pass carries over
📊 Higher density — some passes scale down, none disappear

Why: the worked example is one case of the framework, not the whole territory — the same four levers, math included, apply to a different context with different numbers.
items.learnMore:
The framework, not just the example

Flipping to a dark theme swaps which luminance is "L1" (lighter) and which is "L2" (darker) in the ratio formula, and a gray that passed against white has to be recomputed against the new dark background — the same formula, new inputs, no shortcut for reusing the old answer. A higher-density admin view usually keeps type-scale and contrast passes close to untouched (hierarchy and legibility don't get cheaper just because there's more content) while the spacing pass shrinks its step size — spacing is the lever most directly in tension with "more on screen."

Common mistake

Assuming a contrast pass done in light mode "just works" in dark mode because the same colors are reused — the ratio has to be recomputed against the new background.
